pageTitle: Token buckets, explained with a bag of tickets
title: The bouncer with a bag of tickets
subtitle: A hands-on tour of token-bucket rate limiting, in six short steps.

paras: Your API is popular. One client starts hammering it with thousands of requests a second, and everyone else's requests queue up behind them. You need a way to say slow down that still lets normal users move fast.

The obvious rule, at most N requests per second, punishes honest bursts. A phone app that wakes up and syncs ten things at once gets blocked, while a bot that sends exactly N per second sails through.

Picture a bouncer with a bag of tickets. Every request costs a ticket. Tickets drip into the bag at a steady rate, and the bag has a fixed size. Show up after a quiet spell and you can spend a handful at once. Keep hammering and you wait for the drip.

The bag is the bucket, tickets are tokens. Two numbers describe it: how fast tokens drip in (the rate) and how many the bag holds (the burst). A request takes one token if there is one, or gets refused.
Fire requests one at a time and watch the level drop and refill. Then fire a burst and see the bag empty out.

Here's the catch. A big bucket lets through a big burst, which is exactly the spike you were trying to prevent. A tiny bucket blocks the honest phone app. There is no setting that is right for every client.
Play with the two sliders and try to find a setting that lets the phone app sync but stops the bot.

origin.intro: The token bucket comes from computer networking, where it was used to control how fast a link could send packets and how big a burst it could absorb.

timeline.label: The problem
timeline.text: Networks in the 1980s needed a way to let a sender burst briefly without letting it flood the link.

timeline.label: The naive fix
timeline.text: Cap the sending rate at a fixed number of packets per second. Fair, but it throws away the burst capacity that real traffic needs.

timeline.label: The insight
timeline.text: Separate the two knobs: an average rate and a burst size. Tokens accumulate while the sender is quiet, so a quiet sender earns the right to burst.

timeline.label: Since then
timeline.text: The idea moved from routers to web APIs. It was standardised for ATM networks in 1994 and is now a common default in API gateways.

origin.takeaway: The trade: you accept short bursts in exchange for a simple, predictable average. The bucket size is the size of the burst you are willing to eat.

uses.intro: Anywhere something has to be fair over time but forgiving in the moment.

items.title: Linux traffic control
items.text: The kernel's traffic shaping tools use token buckets to limit bandwidth per queue.

items.title: API gateways
items.text: Amazon API Gateway describes its throttling in terms of a rate and a burst, which is a token bucket.

items.title: Video streaming
items.text: Players use a bucket to smooth out chunks so playback does not stutter.

uses.caveat: What it can't do: it limits one client at a time, so it does nothing about total load across all clients, and clocks that drift between servers can let a client double-spend tokens.
